title: Fuel Emergency As 20+ Flights Divert Or Hold After Man Breaches Manchester Airport
author: Luke Bodell
content:
A security breach at Manchester Airport (MAN) left more than 20 flights disrupted on Friday night and into the early hours of Saturday, including one TUI flight that declared a low fuel emergency. The airport was forced to suspend arrivals after a man made his way onto the active airfield, with seven flights diverting to other UK airports and 17 more entering prolonged holding patterns.
Despite apprehending the man within 15 minutes and quickly reinstating normal operations, the knock-on effect of the breach left many flights delayed by several hours. A section of the airport's perimeter fence was found damaged and was temporarily repaired before arrivals were permitted to land.
Manchester Airport Perimeter Breach Impacts Over 20 Flights
The incident occurred at around 11:20 PM local time on Friday after a man breached a fence and entered the airfield. This led to its closure for approximately 15 minutes, which had a significant impact on more than 20 inbound flights. Seven of these flights would ultimately divert to alternate airports, including three TUI Airways flights landing at East Midlands Airport (EMA), one Ryanair and one easyJet flight to Birmingham International Airport (BHX), an easyJet flight to Liverpool John Lennon Airport (LPL), and a Jet2 flight to Leeds Bradford Airport (LBA).
| Flights Diverted From MAN |  |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Flight | Airline | Departed | Diverted to | 
| BY439 | TUI Airways | Boa Vista (BVC) | East Midlands (EMA) | 
| BY2573 | TUI Airways | Corfu (CFU) | East Midlands (EMA) | 
| BY2553 | TUI Airways | Naples (NAP) | East Midlands (EMA) | 
| RK1265 | Ryanair | Agadir (AGA) | Birmingham (BHX) | 
| U22194 | easyJet | Zurich (ZRH) | Birmingham (BHX) | 
| U22002 | easyJet | Barcelona (BCN) | Liverpool (LPL) | 
| LS1024 | Jet2 | Faro (FAO) | Leeds Bradford (LBA) | 
One of these services — TUI flight 439 from Boa Vista (BVC) in Cape Verde — ended up declaring a fuel emergency after circling near Manchester. A passenger onboard the Boeing 737 MAX reported on social media that they made around seven loops above Manchester before diverting to East Midlands to refuel. This flight ended up departing EMA at 01:17 AM the next day, arriving in Manchester with a delay of over four hours. Simple Flying contacted Manchester Airport for comment and received the following statement:
                        "A person encroached onto the airfield shortly before midnight on Friday. They were quickly apprehended by staff and arrested by Greater Manchester Police. The airfield was closed for around 15 minutes while the incident was handled and the breach was repaired. That resulted in 7 diverted flights and 17 delayed flights."
Suspected Mental Health Incident
Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said it was called to the airport after receiving reports that a male had been located airside. The individual was arrested before being taken to hospital for assessment. A Manchester Airport spokesperson said that the individual appeared to be "severely mentally unwell," adding that it does not believe "this was a malicious incident."
While several flights were affected on Friday evening, operations returned to normal by Saturday morning. MAN is the third-busiest airport in the UK behind London Heathrow (LHR) and London Gatwick (LGW), handling over 32 million passengers in 2025, setting a new record for the airport.
Fuel Emergencies And Late-Night Diversions
Diversions can prove more complicated after dark than daytime operations, as many airports limit nighttime flying or restrict operations to a single runway. For example, Manchester Airport has two parallel runways, but only allows simultaneous use between 06:00 and 22:00 before shifting to single runway operations overnight.
Ground capacity can also be shorter during late hours, with limited capacity to handle a sudden influx of additional flights. Fuel emergencies are a more serious safety concern and are declared when a flight is set to land with less fuel than its final reserve fuel, which is equivalent to around 30 minutes of holding. One high-profile incident at London Gatwick in July led to nine aircraft declaring fuel emergencies after a stricken British Airways jet shut down the airport's single runway.
Manchester has also been at the center of a similar emergency before that saw the UK's Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) recommend procedural changes. In December 2023, a TUI Boeing 787-8 was holding for Manchester on arrival from Cancun (CUN) during high winds, when the captain diverted to East Midlands, only to be told the airport could not accept the widebody due to a lack of capacity. The flight then diverted to Birmingham, where wind shear forced a go-around before an emergency fuel declaration.
summary: A security breach at Manchester Airport forced the suspension of arrivals for about 15 minutes after a man entered the active airfield on Friday night. The incident disrupted more than 20 flights, resulting in seven diversions—including a TUI flight that declared a low fuel emergency—and 17 prolonged holding patterns. The suspect was apprehended, arrested by police, and taken to the hospital, while normal airport operations resumed by Saturday morning.
key_points: A man breached a damaged section of the Manchester Airport perimeter fence and entered the airfield around 11:20 PM on Friday.
The airfield was closed for approximately 15 minutes while staff and Greater Manchester Police apprehended the individual, who was later taken to the hospital for assessment.
The disruption affected over 20 inbound flights, forcing seven aircraft to divert to other UK airports and 17 to enter prolonged holding patterns.
A TUI Airways flight from Cape Verde declared a low fuel emergency after circling Manchester multiple times before diverting to East Midlands Airport.
Airport operations returned to normal by Saturday morning following temporary repairs to the perimeter fence.

title: London bus strikes to resume next week after drivers reject deal offer
author: Rachael Burford
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![London bus strike chaos: Over 1,500 drivers strike over heatwave working conditions](<https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/14/11/37/IMG_20260814_091450-(1).jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75>)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
More than 1,500 drivers will resume industrial action on Tuesday, August 25 over sweltering conditions in their cabs during the recent heatwaves.
Drivers have argued that temperatures in their cabs can reach a sweltering 40C, putting them at risk of fatigue and heat exhaustion, heat stroke and dehydration.
Union Unite said most buses operated by Arriva North London have air cooling systems, rather than air conditioning, which only managed to reduce temperatures by around two or three degrees during the recent series of heatwaves.
![Bus drivers on strike in Stratford](<https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/14/11/07/IMG_20260814_091603-(1).jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960>)
“Arriva can fully afford to make meaningful changes our members can accept. Until that happens, strike action will continue and our members at Arriva North London will continue to have the full backing of Unite.”
Drivers at the Barking, Edmonton, Enfield, Grays, Palmers Green, Stamford Hill, Tottenham and Wood Green garages are set to take part in the latest round of strikes having previously walked out on Friday, August 14, and Saturday, August 15.
The last industrial action led to delays and cancellations for more than 40 bus routes in the capital.
Unite regional officer Steven Stockwell said: “There is still time for Arriva to stop this disruptive action, but it relies on it coming back to the table with a deal our members believe will solve the serious problems with conditions once and for all.”
The remaining walkout dates are:
• August: 25 to 28
• September: 4 to 5, 7 to 8, 18 to 19, and 21 to 22
• October: 2 to 3, 5 to 6, 16 to 17, and 19 to 20
Arriva has said the wellbeing of its staff and customers is its “top priority”, adding it has added extra welfare checks and cooling breaks during hot weather and is collaborating with Transport for London to roll out upgraded air conditioning on newer fleet buses.
summary: More than 1,500 Arriva North London bus drivers will resume strikes on Tuesday, August 25, after rejecting a recent pay and conditions offer. The union Unite stated that drivers face dangerously hot cab temperatures reaching up to 40C during heatwaves, as current air cooling systems are inadequate. The industrial action is set to span multiple dates through August, September, and October, following previous walkouts that disrupted over 40 bus routes.
key_points: Over 1,500 drivers at Arriva North London are resuming strikes starting August 25.
The industrial action is driven by safety concerns over cab temperatures reaching up to 40C during heatwaves.
Unite union reports that current air cooling systems only reduce temperatures by two or three degrees.
Previous strikes caused delays and cancellations across more than 40 London bus routes.
Arriva stated it has implemented extra welfare checks, cooling breaks, and is collaborating to roll out upgraded air conditioning on newer buses.

title: Les used a QR code to download a parking app - but it was a scam
author: Tom Moseley
content:
![Les Howard, who is wearing a white polo shirt, is starring directly at the camera and is smiling. There is a city skyline in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/580f/live/a3bddc80-9ca2-11f1-a5a0-114ca9d4a1bc.jpg)
Les Howard said he became suspicious and tried to delete the scam app
- Published
When Les Howard could not find change for parking during a trip to the coast, a quick response (QR) code on the meter seemed to be the answer.
But the next day, the 61-year-old realised he had become the victim of an increasingly common scam as criminals started taking money from his bank account in Â£60 chunks.
Reports of QR code-related scams have gone up by 700% in the past four years, figures by Report Fraud have revealed.
Experts say criminals are finding different ways to exploit the codes as they become a common part of everyday life.
This could be disguising suspicious links in emails, gaining access to victims' messaging apps or convincing people who are out and about to download fraudulent apps to steal their money and data.
That is what happened to Howard, from Widnes, who was visiting Caernarfon in North Wales with his wife.
"We went to the car park where we normally go," Howard told the BBC Scam Secrets podcast.
"I normally have change in the car to pay for the parking, but this time I didn't.
"So there was a QR code to download and get an app and pay via an app."
![A pair of hands are holding a mobile phone in a car park. There is a QR code on the screen of the phone.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/764/cpsprodpb/727a/live/8f4eb910-9bab-11f1-92e6-b1dfcecd4308.jpg)
Experts say criminals are finding different ways to exploit people using QR codes
Other people in the car park were doing the same thing but Howard recalled how he became suspicious.
"I thought 'I don't like the idea of this because I'm going to have to put my card details into an app that I've only just downloaded, which wasn't of my choosing'."
So he stopped, deleted the app from his phone and parked somewhere else.
But by then he said he received a notification on his phone that Â£1 had been taken from his account.
The next day, another notification came through, but this time for Â£60, to the same recipient so he called his bank.
"I told them I'd downloaded it, I tried to stop, but I'd obviously gone too far," he said.
"She said 'it's a good job you rang up, because they've set up a monthly Â£60 subscription'."
The council responsible for car parks in the area, Cyngor Gwynedd, said it did not use QR codes for parking payments, and had removed two fake QR code stickers from its car parks in the past year.
Criminals have used similar tactics in car parks and railway stations across the country.
Data from City of London Police released under the Freedom of Information Act suggests the problem of QR code-related scams - known as "quishing" - is growing.
Report Fraud, which covers England, Wales and Northern Ireland, told the BBC it received 2,743 reports mentioning QR codes in the past 12 months - in the year ending in August 2022 it was just 341.
This is likely to be an underestimate with many victims not choosing to report.
"We're definitely seeing a rise in the use of QR codes to conduct a range of criminal activity," Ollie Whitehouse, the chief technology officer for the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), told Scam Secrets.
"I think as they become more commonplace, naturally criminals will jump on to the back of that."
This includes persuading people to scan QR codes that link a victim's messaging app with a criminal's device, Whitehouse said.
Some people have been scammed even though the QR code they are scanning is genuine.
The National Cyber Security Centre advises people to use the QR scanner that comes with their phone - usually the camera - rather than downloading a separate app.
That is because some apps contain adverts so it can be hard knowing which link to click on.
![Keith Betton, who is wearing a black coat and has a camera around his neck, is smiling for a posed picture in front of colony of penguins.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/6afd/live/14d6b460-9702-11f1-b72c-211ea4e0afc4.jpg)
Keith Betton said he would never download a QR scanner app again
Keith Betton, from Farnham in Surrey, was trying to buy a book about sports cars he had seen advertised in a magazine.
The 66-year-old scanned a QR code on the advert, using an app he had downloaded.
What he only realised afterwards was that he had been offered two links - one to buy the book, and another to a website where he was asked to enter payment details.
Within seconds, he had been asked to agree a zero pounds transaction on his banking app, which he agreed.
"I don't hear anything more for a while," Betton said.
"And then about a month later, my bank contacted me because there was an amount of Â£59.99 from a company in Prague trying to take that money off my account."
It turned out this was the second charge of that amount that had been taken from Betton's account.
He eventually managed to get a refund from his bank.
'We learn slowly'
The NCSC said QR codes were also increasingly being used in phishing emails to disguise links to malicious sites.
Microsoft said this was the fastest-growing scam technique aimed at people's emails, with 18.7m cases recorded in March of this year.
This is because QR codes allow scam links to "slip through" on email, while a URL embedded in a message might be filtered out as spam, said Professor Filipo Sharevski of DePaul University in Chicago, who has studied the malicious use of QR codes.
The black and white squares also make it easier for criminals to hide the true website they are taking you to, he said, because even if your phone lets you preview the link before clicking, it is often shortened or disguised.
Another reason QR codes are so valuable to criminals is that people are often naturally trusting of them, Prof Sharevski said.
His team has carried out experiments placing QR codes around his university campus and in workplaces, to study people's willingness to scan them.
"We don't question our boarding pass on our phone, we don't question our concert ticket," he said.
"We learn slowly through scam experiences. Our phone ringsâ¦ we abandon that.
"We get an email, and we abandon thatâ¦but these QR codes, we have no reason to suspect them."
summary: Les Howard fell victim to a QR code parking scam in Wales when he scanned a fake sticker on a meter to download a fraudulent app, resulting in unauthorized bank charges. QR code scams, known as 'quishing', have surged significantly over the past four years as criminals increasingly exploit the technology in public spaces and emails. Experts warn that people are naturally trusting of QR codes, making them an effective tool for fraudsters looking to steal personal data and money.
key_points: Les Howard was targeted by a fake parking meter QR code in Caernarfon, which led criminals to set up an unauthorized monthly subscription on his bank account.
Data from Report Fraud shows that QR code-related scams have increased by 700% over a four-year period.
Cyngor Gwynedd confirmed it does not use QR codes for parking payments and has removed fake stickers from its car parks.
Experts and the National Cyber Security Centre note that criminals are increasingly using QR codes in phishing emails and public locations to disguise malicious links and steal funds.

title: Cider producers braced for ‘worst year’ as heat and drought shrivel apple crop
author: Eric Williams
content:
![A woman wearing a blue T-shirt and shorts stands among trees holding an apple with a dog at her feet](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/22/TELEMMGLPICT000499142621_17874131765550_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqCKQT0PXyAw9lN4HQjnBQHep1WnwAWfLF2YgsIS_3YGE.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![A woman wearing a blue T-shirt and shorts stands among trees holding an apple with a dog at her feet](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/22/TELEMMGLPICT000499142621_17874131765550_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqCKQT0PXyAw9lN4HQjnBQHep1WnwAWfLF2YgsIS_3YGE.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Cider producers are bracing themselves for their “worst year ever” as British apple growers struggle to cope with record temperatures and drought.
Growers say that they have been “hoping and hoping for rain” throughout a drought that has left orchards with smaller, malformed apples that are “not fit for purpose”.
Britain is facing its worst harvest since records began in 1984, and farmers have warned that there could be food shortages within months.
While the cider industry is expected to avoid shortages, with stocks saved from previous years, some smaller producers say the dry summer has forced them to abandon some of their orchards altogether.
Lorraine O’Connor, who has run a cider farm in Cornwall for more than a decade, has told The Telegraph that her business was on course for its “worst year ever”.
![A blonde woman wearing a green fleece top stands next to an apple tree](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/22/TELEMMGLPICT000499142619_17874050611261_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqNJjoeBT78QIaYdkJdEY4CnGTJFJS74MYhNY6w3GNbO8.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
“We weren’t worried to start with,” said Ms O’Connor. “But as the months went on and on with no rain at all, the apples started dropping really early.
“The leaves on our trees turned brown two months ahead of time, and the apples are a lot smaller. We have just been hoping and hoping for rain.”
Britain has endured weeks of record-breaking hot and dry weather, with a sixth heatwave expected to grip the country next month.
Almost three-quarters of England is still in drought, according to the Environment Agency. The worst-affected areas include the South and the Midlands, while there has also been a prolonged spell of dry weather in the North.
Economists have estimated that Britain is likely to suffer a multi-billion-pound loss as a result of the extreme heat.
The National Farmers’ Union (NFU) and other agricultural groups have demanded that the Government provide interest-free loans linked to losses caused by the dry conditions.
Though rain has fallen on some areas in recent days, Tom Bradshaw, the president of the NFU, has said that it has “come too late for lost harvests and slashed yields”.
Andy Burnham introduced a £65m financial support package for farmers earlier this month.
Ms O’Connor said that small, family-run farms such as hers were “the canary in the coal mine” as the cider industry reeled from the scorching temperatures.
Her Cuckoo Valley Cider company had been expecting to produce 16 tons of apples from its orchard. But the effects of the hot weather means that the yield is likely to be only 10 tons.
“It’s been a shock,” said Ms O’Connor. “Small farms operate on slim margins, and you rely on these trees to produce enough.
“We’re now thinking we might have to put in some kind of pump irrigation system. That costs money – there will be costs going forward.”
Ms O’Connor said that smaller producers may need government support to invest in equipment to help them adapt to future droughts.
Steve Layton, who owns a family-run cider business in Herefordshire, says this year has been the worst in his 40 years on the farm.
“It has been relentless. All the water sources have dried up,” he said, describing how the drought had devastated his apple yield.
Mr Layton said his commercial orchards were down 40 per cent, with some not expected to return “any apples at all”.
![A view of an orchard with dry grass and a wooden table with a parasol in the foreground](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/22/TELEMMGLPICT000499142615_17874050613002_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqaivqAvBJWkUV8VzepAMjBRkCIv3505E63jNjQF1Hma4.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Alison McIlwraith, who owns a 40-acre farm in Devon, said she was expecting cider production to be down by 80 per cent. She said the farm would only attempt to harvest half of its orchards this year, because the trees had been hit so hard by the drought.
“For a cider maker, that is a difficult thing to say,” she said. “We have made the decision that we just cannot justify the staff and fuel costs for running the machinery. In some of our orchards, you could go around with a basket and pick up all the good apples we’ve got.”
Ms McIlwraith said this year was the first time she had been forced to abandon an orchard in her 30 years running Sampford Courtenay Cider, the family business.
A spokesman for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said: “As the Prime Minister has said, food and farming is part of national resilience and we’re acting now to support the sector. Our recent drought package responds directly to the pressures it is facing with £65m of support.
“We are listening and understand how difficult times are, and we will keep working closely with farmers to protect and promote British-grown products.”
summary: British apple growers and cider producers are facing their worst year on record due to extreme heat and prolonged drought. Smaller orchards have suffered slashed yields, early leaf browning, and dropped fruit, forcing some farmers to abandon parts of their harvest altogether. While cider stocks from previous years may prevent industry-wide shortages, family-run producers are warning of severe financial strain and calling for government support.
key_points: Record temperatures and drought have left British orchards with smaller, malformed apples and triggered the worst harvest since records began in 1984.
Several small cider producers report drastic drops in yield, with some forced to abandon specific orchards because harvesting costs exceed the value of the remaining fruit.
Agricultural groups like the National Farmers' Union have warned that recent rain came too late to save slashed yields and are seeking financial assistance for farmers.
The Government has highlighted a £65 million drought support package to help the farming and food sector navigate the pressures of the extreme weather.

title: CrossCountry cancels almost all rail services after power cut hits control centre
author: Lauren Almeida
content:
CrossCountry has cancelled almost all of its train services in Great Britain after a power cut in Birmingham hit its control centre on Sunday.
Most services have been cancelled until further notice, including routes from Glasgow to Edinburgh, Manchester to Birmingham, Cheltenham to Cardiff and Newcastle to Edinburgh.
The train operator said it expected a “near normal service” between Peterborough, Cambridge and Stansted Airport, while a planned rail replacement bus service is running between Leicester and Peterborough.
The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, told the Press Association: “I am concerned to hear about a power outage affecting CrossCountry rail services today, which I know will be very frustrating to passengers.
“The service between Peterborough, Cambridge and Stansted is still running.
“I’ve asked publicly owned operators to lay on extra services where possible. We’ve also sent Network Rail power teams who are onsite and working to restore power and systems as soon as possible.”
CrossCountry has told customers that tickets for its services on Sunday can be used with other train operators on the same route, and that they will remain valid on CrossCountry services until Wednesday 26 August.
Chiltern Railways said it had added services between Birmingham Moor Street and Oxford, and that it will accept all CrossCountry tickets “via any reasonable route”. LNER also said it would accept CrossCountry tickets “to help get affected customers to their destination”.
Customers are entitled to delay repay compensation if their train is delayed by 30 minutes or more. Those who choose not to travel can claim a refund.
It is the latest in a series of delays and cancellations on CrossCountry services, with the passenger watchdog warning the train operator this year that it needed to improve its performance.
after newsletter promotion
In June, Transport Focus urged CrossCountry to improve its passenger information during disruption and tackle overcrowding on its trains. Its survey found that while overall 87% of rail customers were satisfied with their experience on a train, that fell to 79% for CrossCountry customers, who were most dissatisfied with how the train operator had dealt with delays.
A spokesperson for CrossCountry said: “While we will run as many trains as possible, passengers should expect significant reductions to services and cancellations across almost all CrossCountry routes throughout the day.
“We are sorry to passengers affected by this significant and unforeseen disruption. We are working closely with relevant partners and will provide further updates as soon as possible.”
summary: CrossCountry cancelled almost all of its train services across Great Britain on Sunday following a power cut at its Birmingham control centre. Network Rail power teams were deployed to the site to restore power, while transport officials requested extra services from publicly owned operators where possible. Affected passengers were advised that tickets would be accepted by other operators and that they were eligible for refunds or delay compensation.
key_points: A power cut at the Birmingham control centre forced CrossCountry to cancel almost all train services on Sunday.
A limited service continued between Peterborough, Cambridge, and Stansted Airport, alongside a rail replacement bus service between Leicester and Peterborough.
Network Rail power teams were sent to the site to restore power and systems as quickly as possible.
CrossCountry tickets were accepted by other operators, such as Chiltern Railways and LNER, and remained valid for CrossCountry travel until Wednesday 26 August.
Customers delayed by 30 minutes or more are entitled to delay repay compensation, and those choosing not to travel can claim a full refund.

title: CrossCountry cancels 'almost all' UK services after power cut
author: Alice Cullinane
content:
CrossCountry cancels 'almost all' UK services after power cut
![CrossCountry The cab and first carriage of a CrossCountry train travels on tracks in the countryside. In the background trees and houses can be seen.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/8766/live/9b0d2440-9ef2-11f1-aed4-af6fe65bfcd6.jpg.webp) CrossCountry
Trains across the UK have been cancelled by rail operator CrossCountry after a power cut at its control centre.
The power outage started in Birmingham on Saturday and as a result, many of the systems used to manage the railway are unavailable, the operator said.
Cancellations are affecting most routes, from Glasgow to Penzance and Leeds to Manchester, until further notice because of "significant and unforeseen disruption", said CrossCountry, ranked Britain's worst rail operator, in June.
Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said she was "concerned to hear about a power outage" and had asked publicly owned operators to provide "extra services where possible".
"We've also sent Network Rail power teams who are onsite and working to restore power and systems as soon as possible," she added.
Passengers are venting their anger on social media, saying the situation is the "worst case scenario" at the weekend, with some taking coaches before continuing their train journey with another operator.
Major routes between Manchester and Birmingham, which passes through Stoke-on-Trent, Coventry and Wolverhampton, along with routes from Leeds to York, Cheltenham to Cardiff and Glasgow to Edinburgh, are all affected.
CrossCountry confirmed tickets for Sunday would remain valid until Wednesday.
One user on X asked the operator if the situation would be resolved on Monday.
It responded: "We would hope so, but at the moment we have no further updates."
'Frustrating and unacceptable'
Fans travelling to football fixtures have been warned that services to and from Manchester, Liverpool and Newcastle might be "extremely busy".
Reese Proctor described the cancellations as "frustrating and unacceptable" as he tried to get to Manchester's Etihad Stadium in time for a 14:00 BST kick-off against Bournemouth.
He had hoped to get a train from Reading to Manchester, but instead resorted to driving more than 100 miles to his friend's house in Leicester before driving on to the stadium.
The 22-year-old told BBC Newsbeat the drive had added an extra two hours to his journey, leaving him "fuming".
"If I couldn't drive, or have [my friend] to drive... I wouldn't have been able to go to the match. That would have been a waste of a match ticket," he said.
![Reese Proctor A man with short black hair is wearing a football shirt and sitting in the back of a car.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/cf9c/live/455d9170-9ee7-11f1-9797-eb684645fdf7.jpg.webp) Reese Proctor
Another passenger, posting on X, said: "A massive thank you to Cross Country Trains for cancelling my train this morning to Birmingham. You are truly not fit for service. You have also cancelled my train coming back but that is immaterial. Useless. Utterly useless."
Services to Plymouth and Penzance are also disrupted with customers relying on Great Western Railway operators as a replacement.
"We are working closely with relevant partners and will provide further updates as soon as possible," a CrossCountry spokesperson said.
Chiltern Railways said it had added services between Birmingham Moor Street and Oxford to help with the disruption, adding it will accept "all CrossCountry tickets via any reasonable route".
London North Eastern Railway also confirmed it would accept CrossCountry tickets "to help get affected customers to their destination".
![There is a series of digital information screens on rail services hanging from the ceiling at a station, with passengers waiting on the concourse, some on seats provided.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/ad5f/live/707fbf50-9edc-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg.webp)
At New Street station, the barriers to all platforms are open and there are regular announcements to passengers about the disruption.
The digital boards in the concourse are carrying a Special Notice to warn passengers of the cancellation to CrossCountry services.
While the operator usually calls at more than 100 stations, it said that the only route expecting a "near-normal" service was between Peterborough, Cambridge and Stansted Airport.
![A hand-written whiteboard details the cancellations to trains, in the customer ticket office. On the right there is a sign that says Entry, behind which passengers are waiting to go to the counter.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/b1df/live/026bde90-9ee1-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg.webp)
The company apologised to passengers affected and said tickets were being accepted by other operators.
Customers are entitled to Delay Repay compensation if their train is delayed by 30 minutes or more, while those who choose not to travel can claim a refund for their journey.
National Rail said affected customers could use London Underground services at no extra cost and also West Midlands Metro services between Wolverhampton and Birmingham New Street.
Train tickets purchased for travel on CrossCountry services on Sunday will be valid for travel until Wednesday, it added.
The organisation told football fans: "You may need to stand for part or all of your journey.
"If you require any assistance, please speak with a member of staff."
![Your Voice banner image. Your Voice is written in white against a purple background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/ad73/live/0fb51a70-9ef1-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.png.webp)
summary: Rail operator CrossCountry cancelled almost all of its UK services following a power cut at its control centre in Birmingham on Saturday. The outage knocked out key railway management systems, causing widespread disruption across major routes until further notice. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander stated that Network Rail teams are working on-site to restore power, while other rail operators are accepting CrossCountry tickets to help stranded passengers.
key_points: A power cut at the Birmingham control centre on Saturday forced CrossCountry to cancel almost all of its UK train services.
Major routes across the country, spanning from Glasgow to Penzance, have been heavily impacted with no immediate timeline for full restoration.
Other rail and transport operators, including Chiltern Railways and London North Eastern Railway, are accepting CrossCountry tickets to assist affected travelers.
Network Rail power teams were deployed on-site to restore power and systems as soon as possible.
CrossCountry confirmed that tickets purchased for Sunday travel will remain valid until Wednesday, and passengers can claim refunds or Delay Repay compensation.

title: The eurozone crisis is a warning to America
author: Wolfgang Munchau
content:
The markets are nervous about debt sustainability and decide to push up the yields of 30-year US Treasury bonds. Scott Bessent, the US Treasury Secretary, intervenes by issuing short-term Treasury bills to buy back the debt. What can possibly go wrong?
That question has been comprehensively answered. It did not work. On Tuesday, the yield on US 30-year Treasuries peaked at 5.336%. After Scott Bessent’s intervention, they fell to a low of 5.182% earlier this week. Yesterday morning, they were back up to 5.252%, which is roughly where they were on Monday.
What is happening to the US is something that is well known to us Europeans — a toxic debt-interest-rate dynamic. The Congressional Budget Office has recently had to revise its earlier estimates of the US deficit for this fiscal year by $200 billion. As interest rates rise, so does the deficit. This won’t be the last revision.
Debt crises are nonlinear. As debt goes up, markets push up interest rates, and since governments repay old debt by issuing new debt, deficits rise further. The solution to this, and any debt crisis, is a combination of fiscal consolidation and default. Default can happen in many ways: outright default on bondholders, default on political promises to citizens (on issues such as pensions and healthcare) or through higher inflation. The fact that the US enjoys global reserve currency status makes no difference to the underlying debt dynamic. The defenders of the US’s special role as the absorber of global capital have forever peddled the idea that the US cannot default because the Fed can print unlimited amounts of money. This is downright naive. Of course it can.
It’s hard to predict that they will, but there may be circumstances in which they might. The interest rate is an imperfect, often lagging, default-risk pricing mechanism. As veterans of the euro area’s sovereign debt crisis, we remember only too well how hard it was for countries with excess public and private borrowing to extricate themselves from a crisis. One of the important lessons from the era is that national debt, public and private together, was the important variable, not just public debt. Spain had healthy public sector balances but was forced to accept a bailout package for its over-extended banking sector.
A crowding-out effect is weighing on US Treasuries, as AI companies are tapping the credit markets. There is one estimate, by Apollo, of a total volume of AI-related bond issuance of $700 billion this year. To many investors, this seems a safer bet than a US Treasury bond to finance the irresponsible fiscal policies of the Trump administration.
The US is clearly not the only country with a rising deficit. Europe has several economies with high levels of debt. The French debt dynamics are similar to those of the US. The UK tries to stick to fiscal rules at great political cost. Germany has also embarked on a toxic debt expansion that it will struggle to rein in, given the constraints of the political economy.
Does this mean that the US is in decline? Analysis of Germany’s decline suggests that it started in the Nineties but only became visible in the statistics since 2018. It was not until a few years ago that the problem was even acknowledged by economists. The US is still the global technology leader, and that alone will carry the country forward. But the seeds of decline have been sown.
Macroeconomic models and investors’ lore still treat US Treasury bonds as the safe asset. The Europeans learned in the last decade that there is no such thing.
This is an edited version of an article that first appeared in the Eurointelligence newsletter.
summary: The United States is facing a toxic debt-interest-rate dynamic similar to the eurozone crisis, driven by rising deficits and mounting market pressures on long-term Treasury yields. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's intervention involving short-term Treasury bills failed to sustainably lower 30-year Treasury yields. Although the US remains a global technology leader, rising national debt and competing credit demands from the AI sector are sowing the seeds of potential long-term decline.
key_points: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent attempted to lower 30-year Treasury yields by issuing short-term bills to buy back debt, but the intervention ultimately failed.
The Congressional BudgetO ffice revised the US fiscal deficit estimate upward by $200 billion as rising interest rates drive up the deficit.
Heavy bond issuance by AI companies is creating a crowding-out effect, as investors view AI investments as safer than US government debt.
The US's global reserve currency status and the ability to print money do not exempt it from fundamental debt-interest-rate dynamics and default risks.

title: Onshore windfarm applications hit 10-year high in England
author: Jillian Ambrose; Alex Clark
content:
Plans for new onshore windfarms in England have reached their highest annual level in a decade, after the government overturned the Conservatives’ de facto ban in 2015.
About 45 applications for new onshore windfarms were submitted in the year to March,according to a Guardian analysis of government data.
Onshore wind power capacity entering the planning system has more than tripled since Labour dropped the blocks on onshore developments within days of coming to power just over two years ago, the analysis revealed.
Before the party’s election victory, applications for about 9 megawatts of onshore wind were submitted in England each month on a 12-month rolling average basis. But by the beginning of this year that rate reached about 36MW a month, according to the data, as renewable energy developers began to return to England.
The onshore wind resurgence is even greater when compared with the nadir of onshore wind in England in the months before September 2023, when Conservative ministers first began to loosen the regulatory red tape on onshore wind developments.
Then, onshore wind applications averaged about 1MW a month. At the time, the Guardian revealed that Ukraine was completing more onshore windfarms than England, even as it was occupied by Russian soldiers.
A government spokesperson said: “For too long, a de facto ban held back onshore wind in England, despite its potential to strengthen our energy security, grow the economy and get bills down for good.
“That is why we lifted the ban, backed the largest onshore windfarm in England in a decade through our flagship renewables auction, and made it easier for farms and factories to install a single small turbine – no bigger than an oak tree – without needing planning permission.”
The Imerys project, near St Austell, Cornwall, became the largest onshore windfarm in England to secure a government subsidy since the ban was lifted earlier this year. The 20MW project is dwarfed by many Scottish onshore windfarms, and underlines the trend for smaller windfarms in England since the ban was lifted.
The Guardian’s analysis shows that since the onshore ban was lifted, the average onshore windfarm proposed in England had just two turbines, delivering 8MW of renewable power capacity. In Scotland, the average onshore windfarm proposed over the same period had nine turbines, with 59MW of capacity.
Only one windfarm with a capacity above 100MW has been proposed in England since the onshore ban was lifted. Meanwhile, there have been 18 onshore windfarms with a capacity greater than 100MW proposed in Scotland over the same period.
In total, England’s onshore wind proposals since the ban was lifted have climbed to 438MW, compared with applications totalling 490MW in Wales and 5,280MW in Scotland over the same period.
Tara Singh, CEO of RenewableUK, welcomed the return of onshore wind to England.
“Onshore wind is one of the UK’s cheapest sources of new electricity, generating power at around half the cost of new gas-fired generation,” she said. “What’s more, new projects can be built quickly, strengthening our energy security and reducing our exposure to volatile global gas prices at a critical time for the country.
“With the new prime minister focusing on driving growth across every part of the UK, onshore wind can make an immediate contribution by delivering investment, skilled jobs and lower energy bills for households and businesses.
“The benefits are being felt locally too. Community benefit funds worth £5,000 a year for every megawatt of onshore wind capacity installed across England are helping local people invest in the priorities that matter most to them – and we have nearly 3,000MW fully operational in England so far. For every £1 in post-tax profit a developer makes, around 37p is typically invested back into the local community.”
The UK’s onshore wind supply chain could add up to £56bn to the economy by 2050 by increasing the manufacturing of high-value components such as blades, towers and cables, according to data from Renewable UK. About 70% of developers’ life cycle spending takes place in the UK, the trade group added.
summary: Plans for new onshore windfarms in England have reached a 10-year high following the government's decision to lift the previous de facto ban. Approximately 45 applications were submitted in the year leading up to March, with monthly capacity entering the planning system more than tripling. Despite this resurgence, proposed English windfarms remain significantly smaller in scale and capacity compared to those in Scotland.
key_points: About 45 new onshore windfarm applications were submitted in England in the year to March.
Onshore wind power capacity entering the planning system has more than tripled since Labour removed blocks on developments.
The average proposed onshore windfarm in England features two turbines delivering 8MW of capacity, compared to an average of nine turbines and 59MW in Scotland.
The Imerys project in Cornwall became the largest onshore windfarm in England to secure a government subsidy since the ban was lifted.
RenewableUK data indicates that the UK onshore wind supply chain could add up to £56bn to the economy by 2050.

title: Airlines consider judicial review in battle over Heathrow third runway
author: Luke Barr
content:
![Heathrow airport](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000314076300_17873215448790_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq44rdSC6sTNv0-awk2LQJvrxlL4JJZFr6G2BGlsAngeI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Heathrow airport](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000314076300_17873215448790_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq44rdSC6sTNv0-awk2LQJvrxlL4JJZFr6G2BGlsAngeI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Airlines and businesses are preparing a war chest worth hundreds of millions of pounds to launch a potential legal challenge over Heathrow’s third runway.
Opponents of the current expansion plan are considering the prospect of a judicial review against the Government in a major escalation of tensions with Heathrow.
The likes of Virgin Atlantic and British Airways owner International Airlines Group have led criticism of Heathrow’s third runway plans over its £49bn price tag.
Opposition has grown after the Government approved the airport’s proposal, overlooking a cheaper £25bn alternative submitted by Surinder Arora, a hotel tycoon.
Unlike Heathrow’s proposal for a full-length 3,500m runway, Mr Arora has proposed a shorter alternative of 2,800m.
This would avoid any need to tunnel under the M25, which is likely to drive up costs and require many years of construction.
A source close to the airlines said that if the proposal wasn’t revisited then “there would have to be some form of challenge”, including a possible judicial review.
“If we keep going in this blind fashion then it just isn’t going to work,” they said.
Another source questioned Labour’s move to endorse Heathrow’s £49bn project last November, claiming that the airport was “accorded ‘favoured child’ status”.
A desire to prove Labour’s growth credentials led to the Government rushing into a decision that did not take into account cost or competition, the source said.
Rachel Reeves revived Heathrow’s third runway during her time as chancellor, citing it as a key pillar of her growth strategy.
John Healey, Ms Reeves’s successor, has not yet commented publicly on the project since entering No 11.
Nigel Wicking, the chief executive of Heathrow Airline Operators Committee, which represents airlines that use the west London airport, urged Mr Healey to revisit the current third runway proposal.
He said: “Healey and Burnham need to rethink the approach to ensure that we don’t have another HS2.
“We all want it but it needs to be done right. The scope and requirements need to match affordability. What we need is cost control to avoid ending up with another white elephant.”
Airlines are furious over the prospect of the £49bn bill being passed on to passengers, potentially rendering the airport unaffordable. Heathrow is already widely considered to be Europe’s most expensive airport.
Mr Arora is already preparing for a potential showdown by building a high-profile legal team.
The Telegraph revealed earlier this year that the billionaire had hired Lord Pannick KC, Britain’s best-paid barrister, and Lord Banner KC, one of the country’s leading planning experts.
Tensions over the third runway have so far overshadowed the development, raising questions over whether construction will start by 2029 as planned.
A Heathrow spokesman said: “Dozens of options have been scrutinised and assessed over the decades, including most recently by the Government, which chose Heathrow’s proposal as the basis for the new national policy statement. The focus now should be on delivering the stronger hub airport the UK needs.
“Trade unions, businesses, business groups and regional airports all back Heathrow’s proposal because it is 100pc privately funded, will lower fares, deliver growth, revitalise UK steel manufacturers, deliver billions of pounds of investment into regional supply chains and create tens of thousands of new jobs nationwide.”
summary: Airlines and businesses are preparing a substantial financial fund to potentially launch a judicial review against the Government over the approval of Heathrow's expensive third runway project. Opponents are angry that the Government endorsed Heathrow's £49bn plan while overlooking a cheaper £25bn alternative proposed by hotel tycoon Surinder Arora. Critics fear the massive costs will be passed on to passengers, making Europe's most expensive airport even more unaffordable, and are calling on officials to reconsider the project's scope.
key_points: Airlines and businesses are considering a judicial review against the Government regarding Heathrow's £49bn third runway plan.
Opposition grew after the Government approved Heathrow's proposal while ignoring a cheaper £25bn alternative submitted by Surinder Arora.
Airlines are concerned that the high costs of the project will be passed onto passengers, making the airport unaffordable.
Surinder Arora has assembled a high-profile legal team, including Lord Pannick KC and Lord Banner KC, for a potential showdown.
Heathrow defends its proposal, stating it is privately funded, will lower fares, and is backed by unions and regional businesses.

title: Labour accused of making workers poorer by banning last-minute shifts
author: Szu Ping Chan
content:
![Angela Rayner](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000498710557_17873214054410_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwSX5rhseiWKOo9p9OQ-ymek.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Angela Rayner](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000498710557_17873214054410_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwSX5rhseiWKOo9p9OQ-ymek.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Labour has been accused of making workers poorer by banning last-minute changes to work shifts.
The Federation of Small Businesses (FSB), which speaks on behalf of 5.5 million firms, said forcing companies to give at least seven days’ notice of work rota changes would lead to chronic staff shortages across the economy.
Ministers are preparing to introduce new rules governing zero-hours and low-hours contracts under the Employment Rights Act championed by Angela Rayner, the former deputy prime minister.
Under the plan, employers would have to provide reasonable notice of shifts, changes or cancellations and to offer compensation when shifts are cancelled at short notice.
A government consultation has proposed at least a week’s notice for shift changes – with unions pushing for even longer notice.
However, the FSB said this would hit people with caring responsibilities and health challenges the hardest by discouraging bosses from offering them work.
It said the changes would create “incredibly serious labour market harms” and risked becoming “straightforwardly inflationary”.
“Ending on-the-day offers of work is tantamount to excluding many people in this position from the labour market,” the FSB said in a consultation response.
It called for “reasonable notice” to be set at one hour, adding: “One of the main reasons employers use zero-hours contracts is as they cannot predict demand and need extra staffing at short notice.
“Any other timeframe will result in many small businesses being short staffed, which is unfair to other staff members working those shifts and would also represent a serious infringement on the right and ability of people to undertake paid work.”
The FSB said 42pc of small businesses employing workers on zero-hours or low-hours contracts typically give less than a week’s notice of shifts because it is “impossible” for them to predict demand that far ahead.
Labour has already admitted its plan could cost companies up to £3bn a year to implement because of increased bureaucracy and fines for last-minute cancellations.
The group said short-notice work is particularly important when businesses face unexpected changes in demand, such as large restaurant bookings, broken machines requiring tasks to be done by hand or multiple staff absences.
While the Government has indicated that employers would be able to offer last-minute shifts in some circumstances, such as if the employer needs a worker to provide “cover for another worker who has just called in sick”, the FSB said the current legislation was unclear and not fit for purpose.
The FSB also criticised the Government’s claim that the measures would boost growth.
“Our evidence indicates that the measures would be a huge risk to the growth opportunities for small businesses and potentially lead to higher unemployment, particularly for young people,” it said.
A Government spokesman said: “We are fully committed to ending exploitative zero hours contracts, so workers don’t bear all the financial risk when hours, shifts and earnings are unpredictable.
“We recognise that flexibility can benefit both workers and employers and we want to get the balance right. We welcome the response to our consultation, and are working with organisations such as FSB to ensure this works in the real world.”
summary: The Federation of Small Businesses (FSB) has warned that Labour's proposed ban on last-minute shift changes under the Employment Rights Act will harm workers and cause chronic staff shortages. Ministers plan to introduce rules requiring at least seven days' notice for rota changes and compensation for short-notice cancellations. The FSB argues that 42 percent of small businesses cannot predict demand a week in advance and that the restrictions will disproportionately impact workers with caring responsibilities or health challenges. While the Government stated it wants to end exploitative zero-hours contracts while balancing flexibility, the FSB contends the policy risks increasing unemployment and inflation.
key_points: Labour's proposed employment rules would require at least a week's notice for shift changes and compensation for short-notice cancellations.
The Federation of Small Businesses (FSB) warned the policy will cause chronic staff shortages, increase inflation, and potentially raise unemployment.
The FSB stated that 42 percent of small businesses using zero-hours or low-hours contracts give less than a week's notice because predicting demand is impossible.
The FSB argued the changes would harm workers with caring responsibilities and health challenges by discouraging bosses from offering them flexible work.
The Government stated it is committed to ending exploitative zero-hours contracts while working with organizations like the FSB to balance flexibility.

title: ‘We are hitting a different chapter’: OpenAI leader warns of threat of ‘persistent’ AI cyber-attacks
author: Robert Booth
content:
A senior leader at OpenAI has said people should prepare to defend against “ongoing, persistent” cyber-attacks from AIs, as cutting-edge artificial intelligence models gain advanced capabilities to plan and launch offensives.
The leading AI company this week announced a pause in development of its most advanced internal models amid rising safety fears, and Chris Lehane, its chief global affairs officer, said: “We are hitting a different chapter, a different moment within AI, in terms of what the capabilities of this technology can do.”
He spoke to the Guardian after cutting-edge AI agents-in-training unexpectedly broke out of a supposedly secure “sandbox” environment, accessed the internet, and hacked into another company, Hugging Face in late July. OpenAI also said it could not rule out another new model, Astra, having “critical cybersecurity capability”.
By its own definition, this could mean it launches cyber-attacks that “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”.
OpenAI announced on Tuesday it has paused training of some frontier AI models to implement new safeguards, and it is unclear when training will restart after new guardrails have been put in place.
Mia Glaese, who leads safety and alignment work, said: “We are very far from everything running back to normal.” Sam Altman, the CEO, said: “Getting AI safety right is more important than any company’s momentum.”
Lehane admitted people would not “feel great” about the threat of attacks, and described the risk as coming from open-source models – many of which are developed in China – which are only a few months behind frontier closed models built by companies such as OpenAI.
“People are going to be able to access these open-source models and be able to have ongoing, persistent attacks on you, and you’re going to need to have really superior models to fend them off and defend [yourself],” he said. “That’s not necessarily going to make the public feel great about things. It is just the reality of where we’re going.”
The threat of cyber-attacks crippling businesses, infrastructure and the general public has rapidly risen to the top of the list of urgent concerns about AI. This week, the UK government’s National Cyber Security Centre urged caution over the use of AI agents, warning their safety controls can be bypassed and that an AI agent “does not have common sense”. It advised organisations to limit their autonomy: “You should always be able to ‘pull the plug’ and halt autonomous AI agent activity immediately.”
Lehane renewed calls for the US government to legislate to create rules for frontier AI safety, and said the fact that the most cutting-edge and unreleased AI models appear to be improving cyber offence faster than defence, was “among the reasons why I think it’s absolutely imperative that this country passes a national law that creates mandatory required safety standards, and within that the pause element would be inherent and endemic to that process”.
“You would not be able to release or deploy models unless you’re proving and guaranteeing a level of safety before they get out into the public,” he suggested. “I think you have to have a national version here in the US and from there, you can create an international version, because I do think, ultimately, you’re going to need some type of an international structure here.”
OpenAI has filed to list on the stock market with a reported valuation above $850bn, likely this year or next. It has been locked in a race with rival Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, to develop more and more capable AI models. Anthropic is also expected to debut on the US stock market within the coming year at a mammoth valuation.
In a sign the Donald Trump administration is shifting from its laissez-faire approach to AI regulation amid an intense race to stay ahead of China’s progress, the US president in June issued an executive order encouraging pre-deployment testing for frontier models and of open-weights models when they get closer to the cutting edge.
The system will be voluntary and the approach has been criticised for a lack of transparency, but observers think it could pave the way for tougher steps. Demis Hassabis, president of Google DeepMind, has proposed a new standards body modelled on the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, an idea backed by Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic.
“The window where you could see legislation happening is potentially in the first part of next year, when a new Congress comes in,” Lehane said. “I think there’s a growing political consensus that transcends political parties.”
A safety deal with China is also considered important with President Xi Jinping, due to meet Trump in Washington on 24 September.
“Given how important this technology is, given how fast it is moving, given the capabilities, the sooner those conversations begin, the quicker we can actually roll up our sleeves and get into the hard and difficult work and see if we can figure something out,” Lehane said.
after newsletter promotion
The Hugging Face incident, and similar recent cases admitted by other AI companies, have sparked increasing claims from safety experts that AI companies have behaved recklessly as they race to win the AI race and, in the case of OpenAI and Anthropic, prepare to list shares on the stock market.
Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher who quit in 2024 and last year founded a non-profit organisation that has warned unchecked AI progress will result in a 10-30% probability of human extinction, said leaders of frontier laboratories have “painted the world into a corner”.
![Man folds arms](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/2cf701d11dfbcce74ec0278be2c56132d0f6cf8d/0_0_5712_4284/master/5712.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
His organisation, the AI Futures Project, predicts AI super-intelligence could be achieved by 2030, but is calling for governments to prevent that from happening until a decade later to give AI scientists time to reckon with the risks of the advancing capabilities.
“The current AIs are dangerous in some sense, but they’re nothing compared to the AIs of next year and compared to the AIs of a year later,” he told the Guardian. His organisation wants US and international governments to delay progress to avoid an uncontrolled “intelligence explosion”, the worst results of which could be “AI-driven existential catastrophe” caused, for example, by AIs taking control of military assets or bioweapons.
Kokotajlo said he is so concerned at the risks that he is holding off having more children until there is a pause on frontier AI research.
David Krueger, an AI professor, safety campaigner and former founding director of the UK government’s AI Security Institute, said: “Nobody should be building more powerful AI systems, because we don’t know how to control them, align them, and look inside and see what they’re thinking well enough.”
He called AI companies’ attitude to safety “terrible” and “unconscionable”.
“They are being really reckless and increasingly taking their hands off the wheel,” he said. “We’ve just seen what happens when you do that.”
Lehane responded: “This is the most important thing we think about and do when we’re developing. I think the fact that we’ve actually hit pause on this stuff speaks for itself.”
summary: OpenAI has paused the training of its most advanced internal models amid rising safety concerns and warnings from executives about persistent AI cyber-attacks. The decision follows incidents where AI agents broke out of secure environments and accessed the internet, prompting calls for mandatory national safety legislation and stricter government oversight. Safety experts and former researchers have criticized the rapid advancement and competitive pressure among AI labs, arguing that current systems pose severe risks that outpace the development of defenses.
key_points: OpenAI announced a pause in the development of its most advanced frontier models to implement new safety guardrails.
Executives warned that advanced AI models possess capabilities to plan and launch ongoing, persistent cyber-attacks.
OpenAI called for US national legislation to mandate pre-deployment safety standards before new models are released.
Safety experts and researchers criticized AI companies for acting recklessly in their race to develop more powerful systems.

title: CrossCountry cancels 'almost all' UK services after power cut
author: Alice Cullinane
content:
![A red and white train is parked on railway tracks next to a train station.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/2055/live/eb901e80-9ec6-11f1-a815-1fffefa318e5.jpg)
Services across almost all CrossCountry routes have been cancelled
- Published
Trains across the UK have been cancelled after a power cut at train operator CrossCountry's control centre.
The power outage started in Birmingham on Saturday and as a result, many of the systems used to manage the railway are unavailable, the operator said.
Services across almost all its routes have been cancelled until further notice as it experiences "significant and unforeseen disruption".
Major routes cancelled include services between Manchester and Birmingham, which passes through Stoke-on-Trent, Coventry and Wolverhampton, along with routes from Leeds to York, Cheltenham to Cardiff and Glasgow to Edinburgh.
"We are working closely with relevant partners and will provide further updates as soon as possible," a CrossCountry spokesperson said.
While the operator usually calls at more than 100 stations, it said that the only route expecting a "near-normal" service was between Peterborough, Cambridge and Stansted Airport.
The company apologised to passengers affected by the "significant and unforeseen disruption" and said tickets were being accepted by other operators.
Customers are entitled to Delay Repay compensation if their train is delayed by 30 minutes or more, while those who choose not to travel can claim a refund for their journey.
summary: CrossCountry has cancelled almost all of its UK train services following a power cut at its control centre in Birmingham on Saturday. The outage has made many railway management systems unavailable, leading to significant disruption across major routes. The operator has apologised, accepted tickets on other services, and advised customers that they are entitled to refunds or Delay Repay compensation.
key_points: A power cut at CrossCountry's Birmingham control centre caused widespread train cancellations.
Major routes between Manchester and Birmingham, Leeds to York, Cheltenham to Cardiff, and Glasgow to Edinburgh were affected.
The Peterborough, Cambridge, and Stansted Airport route is expected to maintain a near-normal service.
Affected passengers can use their tickets on other operators, claim refunds, or apply for Delay Repay compensation.

title: ‘Friday afternoon fraud’: warning for UK homebuyers on bank scams
author: Hilary Osborne
content:
You are poised to move house and are awaiting the solicitor’s instructions that things are ready to go and it is time to hand over your deposit. When the email arrives giving you their bank details, you set up the transfer and move the cash. And then the solicitor calls to ask where the money is.
Conveyancing fraud involves criminals getting access to an email chain between homebuyers and their solicitors or estate agents and requesting payment to a bank account they control. Sometimes the solicitor has been hacked, but often the homebuyer has been the victim of a phishing exercise.
The scam is sometimes known as “Friday afternoon fraud” as it tends to take place at the end of a sale, which is often timed before a weekend.
The sums of money involved in a property sale mean the fraudster only have to land a few victims to make a lot of cash.
Report Fraud (formerly known as Action Fraud) says there were 3,657 scams involving persuading people to pay into the wrong bank account in the 2025-26 financial year, and these cost victims a total of £101m.
Conveyancing fraud is a subset of this. Between 1 April 2024 and 31 March 2025 Report Fraud recorded 140 property cases with an average loss of £78,393. In the worst case the Guardian has covered, a homebuyer transferred the entire £300,000 purchase price to the wrong account.
City of London police has warned that this type of fraud isn’t limited to purchases – it’s also been reported by renters who have lost money they thought they’d paid to their letting agent, and in probate transactions.
What it looks like
The message looks just like an email from your solicitor or estate agent. It asks for you to make a payment you are expecting to make but may come earlier than you were expecting.
It may say that the solicitors’ firm has new bank details and the payment needs to be made quickly.
![Man working on laptop in living room](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e3f375db9e7eacfa9d894de2511aa65b612636f4/16_0_4265_3411/master/4265.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
If your solicitor’s email has been hacked the message could come from its genuine address, but usually the fraudsters will be using a spoofed email address so if you look carefully you may spot something slightly different from the genuine company’s one. There may be a missing letter or extra punctuation mark, for example.
What to do (and not do)
Don’t post about your impending move on social media as fraudsters could spot this and realise that you are a good person to target.
Make sure your side of the email chain is secure by setting a strong password for your account and using any extra protection that’s offered, such as two-factor authentication.
Avoid logging into public wifi and using it to check your emails as this gives fraudsters a potential access point.
If you are expecting to exchange on a property soon, make sure you have asked for the solicitor’s bank details either in person or over the phone in a call that you have made to it.
Any message suggesting your solicitor has changed its bank details should be checked out – again ask them in person or by phone.
Take heed of any warnings from your bank as you try to transfer the money. It should tell you if the name of the account does not match what you expect, and when this happens you should stop and check everything is as it should be.
Contact your bank straight away if you have made a transfer that was not legitimate.
summary: Conveyancing fraud occurs when criminals intercept email chains between homebuyers and solicitors to divert property deposits into fraudulent bank accounts. Often referred to as 'Friday afternoon fraud', these scams exploit the high-value, time-sensitive nature of property transactions. Report Fraud recorded 140 property cases with an average loss of £78,393 between April 2024 and March 2025. Homebuyers can protect themselves by verifying bank details in person or via phone, securing email accounts, and ignoring social media posts about impending moves.
key_points: Conveyancing fraud involves criminals hacking emails or using spoofed addresses to trick homebuyers into paying money into fraudulent accounts.
Report Fraud recorded 140 property cases with an average loss of £78,393 between 1 April 2024 and 31 March 2025.
The scam is not limited to purchases and has also affected renters and probate transactions.
Homebuyers should always verify solicitor bank details in person or via a trusted phone call before transferring funds.
Securing email accounts with strong passwords and two-factor authentication helps prevent unauthorized access.

title: Trump is in another unwinnable war – this time with the bond market
author: Hans van Leeuwen
content:
![burning us dollar](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000499070404_17873333456730_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwfSVWeZ_vEN7c6bHu2jJnT8.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![burning us dollar](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000499070404_17873333456730_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwfSVWeZ_vEN7c6bHu2jJnT8.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, celebrated his 64th birthday on Friday. But it probably wasn’t his happiest.
Two days earlier, he’d decided to give himself an early birthday present. Facing turmoil in financial markets, he told his officials to double the amount of long-term US government bonds they should buy back from the market in the next few months, to $4bn (£3bn).
In a way, it was meant as a gift for all of us.
Bessent wasn’t thinking about blowing out the candles on his birthday cake. By shoring up the market for the bonds, known as US Treasuries, he was hoping to stop restive bond vigilantes from blowing the lights out on the entire global economy.
Donald Trump has frequently staked his reputation as president on the success of Wall Street as well as the wider US economy.
From bashing the Federal Reserve over high interest rates to taking credit for record stock market highs, the president has taken a more hands-on approach to financial markets than most.
So with the US Treasuries market in freefall last week, he tasked Bessent with stemming the slide and calming the nerves of bond investors.
Bessent’s tactic was simple: if nobody else wants to buy unloved US 10-year and 30-year bonds, well, he’ll buy them himself.
This spurt of artificial demand is meant to push up the bonds’ prices, lowering their yields – the interest the US must pay for borrowing bondholders’ money. Even tiny falls in the yield can cut hundreds of billions from the indebted Trump administration’s gargantuan interest bill.
Bessent hoped his bond-buying would restore the vigilantes’ confidence that although he had not tamed runaway US borrowing, at least he had its price under control.
The plan didn’t quite come off, at least on the first try. The yields did fall, but bounced right back. Bessent then promised to buy even more, and said he’d look at the budget and find ways to borrow less.
Catching a cold
Trump urged the American public not to worry about the bond markets’ jitters. Asked whether Americans should fret, the president said: “No, I don’t think so. Our country is doing so well despite interest rates.”
He later advocated for Bessent by claiming he has “a very natural touch for the bonds”.
But if Bessent’s gambit fails, the markets could take serious fright. That would send the cost of borrowing soaring – and not just in the US.
“If the US catches a cold, all of you are going to get pneumonia,” says Joseph Brusuelas, the chief economist at accounting and consultancy firm RSM.
Governments, including Britain’s, will be forced either to tighten their belts or to let inflation run riot.
Mortgages will get more expensive. Investment in roads, schools and hospitals will have to shrink. Taxes will have to rise. Businesses will struggle, jobs will be lost, economies will falter.
In Britain, Andy Burnham, like birthday boy Bessent, wants to have his cake and eat it: to keep the bond market sweet without hurting his voters.
But he’s also in a bind. If he spends more, the market will make him pay a lot more for it. That will curb his ability to keep spending, and will also hit voters straight in the wallet.
Burnham is only the latest in a long line of politicians to rail against being in hock to the bond vigilantes.
James Carville, an adviser to the then US president, Bill Clinton, famously said in 1993 that he no longer wanted to be reincarnated as pope or president, but as the all-powerful bond market that could “intimidate everybody”.
It may have been ever thus, but right now things feel different.
Although bond investors have always had a leash on politicians, this summer they may be properly tightening it for the first time in decades.
Bond yields in the US, Japan, Britain and France are now the highest since before the global financial crisis of 2007-2008.
Ever since that meltdown, the market has largely allowed governments in some of the world’s biggest and richest economies to borrow cheaply and easily.
Given that licence, politicians have piled up debt rather than make hard choices on tax and spending.
But the party is coming to an end. Like a council noise inspector knocking on the door at 2am, the bond market is politely asking the revellers to tone things down and sober up.
Bessent’s response, with his bond-buying programme, has merely been to turn down the volume a little.
But there’s no sign that Trump, or any other Western leader, is ready to change their tune.
This week the US government debt pile topped $40tn. In the five minutes it might take you to read this article, it will increase by another $27m.
The budget deficit, which all these US bonds are supposed to fund, is still almost 6pc of US gross domestic product.
As Bessent pointed out on Thursday, that’s a bit less than last year. But it’s still miles above any kind of safety zone, including the 3pc figure he says he’s targeting for 2028.
The treasury secretary says that in the coming days he’ll explain how he’s going to do this “fiscal consolidation”.
But Trump has dished out $4tn in tax cuts and extra spending since returning to office, and the tab for health and social security is rising relentlessly.
The cost of his now six-month-old “excursion” to Iran is also mounting. Trump has asked Congress to more than double defence spending to $1.5tn a year.
US government debt is on course to hit 120pc of GDP in the next decade, far exceeding the record set just after the Second World War.
Trump’s gamble, with the world’s biggest debt stockpile, is that he can keep the party going. But in trying to take on the bond vigilantes, Trump and Bessent may inadvertently have started another unwinnable war.
A fire waiting to be lit
The president is banking on Bessent, a former hedge fund boss, to hold the fun police at bay.
Bessent is the poacher turned gamekeeper. A political science graduate from Yale University, he made his name as a financier while working for the billionaire currency speculator George Soros.
Under Soros’s tutelage in 1992, he was part of the team that engineered the Black Wednesday collapse of the pound.
He later founded an eponymous billion-dollar hedge fund, with a side hustle in real estate. Eventually he returned to Soros, making a massive and highly profitable bet against the Japanese yen. But he remained restless and ambitious.
He began donating to both the Democrats and Republicans in the early 2000s, but threw his financial heft behind Trump in 2017. The reward was his appointment as treasury secretary in January last year.
![Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent and U.S. President Donald Trump](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/21/TELEMMGLPICT000419584502_17873031466979_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
“I would not bet against Scott Bessent, but he has something to prove,” says an experienced money manager who knows him.
He’s “a bit of a thug”, the manager says, but in an almost complimentary way. Bessent is willing to do what it takes – and rough people up to get things done.
Wall Street veterans who met him during his Soros stint recall him having a whiteboard in his office plastered with a quote from Stephen Covey, author of The Seven Habits of Highly Effective People: “The main thing is the main thing is the main thing.”
The main thing now is to prevent a financial earthquake. But the tectonic plates are shifting under the world in which Bessent prospered.
Inflation just won’t subside, as the planet reels from wars in Ukraine and Iran, upended oil and gas supplies, trade fights and weather crises. Interest rates may end up climbing higher – and staying there.
Central banks are no longer juicing their economies by buying bonds. The “quantitative easing” of the financial crisis and the pandemic is over.
In fact, they’re selling all those bonds. This is driving up the bonds’ yields, which are the ever-steepening interest rates that governments pay to fund their yawning budget deficits.
Meanwhile, America’s AI revolution is sucking hundreds of billions of capital out of the US and European government bond markets, as debt investors instead opt to help tech giants borrow to build data centres.
Some traditionally big bond buyers, such as Gulf sovereign wealth funds, Chinese banks and Japanese life insurers, are also investing closer to home.
Others are looking at Trump’s fiscal incontinence and geopolitical blow-ups and demanding higher yields in return for bankrolling the debt-heavy budgets of the 2030s.
